title: AI prediction leads people to forgo guaranteed rewards
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether artificial intelligence can change not only what people decide, but how they decide when they believe a system can predict their behavior. The authors frame the question through a behavioral version of Newcomb’s paradox: if people think an AI has already predicted their choice, will they alter their decision to align with that prediction, even when doing so means giving up a guaranteed reward?

Across four preregistered online experiments with 1,305 adult participants, the researchers manipulated whether the outcome was framed as being determined by an AI predictor or by a random mechanism. In the main task, participants chose between taking a guaranteed payment plus a contingent reward, or taking only the contingent reward. Additional studies tested different AI presentations, interactive versus non-interactive interfaces, vignette-based scenarios beyond the monetary task, and repeated exposure across multiple rounds. The studies were conducted online through Prolific, and one interactive condition used an LLM-based chatbot styled as a predictive agent.

The results showed that framing the outcome as predicted by AI increased the likelihood that participants forwent the guaranteed reward, relative to random framing. The effect generalized across task variants and persisted even when participants received repeated evidence that the AI prediction was not perfectly reliable. The authors argue that perceived predictive authority can create a form of "predictive binding," in which people treat the AI’s forecast as linked to their own future action and adjust behavior accordingly. They conclude that AI may shape decision-making not just by recommending actions, but by altering how people experience their own choices.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a preregistered series of online behavioral experiments with randomized conditions, but it is not an education study and does not evaluate a schooling intervention or learner outcome. The design is strong experimentally, yet the evidence is about general decision behavior in a lab-style task rather than K-12 educational impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a clear behavioral effect of AI prediction on willingness to forgo a guaranteed reward, but it has no direct educational application or student learning outcome. Because the finding is outside the education domain and concerns an abstract economic choice task, its K-12 impact is not established.

interventions.use_case: behavioral experiment testing how AI-predicted choices influence decision-making in a Newcomb's paradox-style task, including an LLM-based chatbot interaction variant and repeated prediction feedback

finding.finding_summary: Across Studies 1 and 2 (combined meta-analytic estimate), framing the situation as predicted by AI increased the odds of forgoing a guaranteed reward by a factor of 3.39 (OR=3.39, 95% CI [2.45, 4.70]) compared with random framing. In Study 1, one-boxing rose from 26.0% (26/100) in the random condition to 41.0% (41/100) in the AI condition, indicating that perceived predictive authority altered choice behavior.
finding.measure: Proportion choosing one-boxing / forgoing guaranteed reward in a monetary choice task
finding.study_size: n=801 across Studies 1 and 2; Study 1 n=200

finding.finding_summary: In Study 4 (n=201), repeated exposure to AI prediction produced divergence by prediction policy: one-boxing remained stable when the AI predicted one-boxing, but declined significantly over time when the AI predicted two-boxing (interaction p=0.002; slope p<0.001 in the two-box condition). Even after five repeated predictive failures, one-boxing in the final round remained 30.6%, still above the random baseline from Study 2 (15.3%; p=0.003), suggesting persistence of the effect despite disconfirmation.
finding.measure: Round-by-round proportion of one-boxing across five repeated task rounds
